lines.watchItem: Accelerator demand is still booked years out: supply-chain sources put order visibility into 2030, quarterly tool demand at roughly 1.9 times the level projected in December 2025, and August revenue up 53.3 percent year over year. Leading-edge wafer-start plans therefore sit against order books that already run past the planning horizon.

Advanced packaging (CoWoS), not wafer output, is named the binding limit on finished AI systems, with monthly capacity around 105,000 to 130,000 wafers by the fourth quarter of 2026, lead times of 52 to 78 weeks and a supply gap still near 20 percent. Realizable accelerator revenue stays tied to how fast those packaging lines come up.

Packaging allocation is pre-booked at more than 85 percent for 2026 and 2027, with one buyer at roughly 60 percent of capacity and Advanced Micro Devices at about 11 percent, or some 105,000 wafers. A single large buyer trimming orders would leave slots that are hard to refill at that scale.

Rival packaging routes are winning real volume: Google has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel bridge packaging for 2028 delivery, Intel reports yields above 90 percent at roughly half the cost of CoWoS, and Samsung and Amkor quote 26 to 39 week waits against 52 to 78 weeks. Shorter quoted waits are the thing to track, since they are what pulls work away.

Custom accelerator programmes are scaling toward merchant size, with Broadcom guiding artificial-intelligence chip revenue from about $58 billion this year to $115 billion in 2027 and $230 billion in 2028, OpenAI's first inference chip built on 3nm, and Microsoft negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 of its own parts for 2027. The leading-node customer base shifts toward model labs and cloud buyers rather than only the two merchant vendors.

Pricing conditions across the chain stay firm: wafer price increases of 3 to 6 percent are reported for 2027 with larger rises possible on AI orders, second-quarter gross margin came in at 67.7 percent on revenue up 36 percent, and the second-largest foundry raised prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders. The exposure is to how long buyers absorb those increases.

Memory costs are moving down the chain and into customer margins, with memory and flash costs up over 300 percent year on year, the leading vendor guiding gross margin to 74 percent plus or minus 50 basis points against a stated floor of 71 to 72 percent, and management flagging a further dip into the low 70 percent range. Thinner customer margins are where any pushback on wafer and packaging prices would show up first.

A growing slice of the order book rests on buyers whose revenue is far behind their commitments: Bain puts the annual industry revenue required by 2031 at $6 trillion against up to $1.8 trillion covered today, and one model lab has signed at least $518 billion of infrastructure spending, about 80 percent of it non-cancelable, while reporting a $42 billion net loss for 2025. Capital-market access at those buyers is the exposure behind today's wafer and packaging bookings.
